blocks.title: The tens
head: Digit
French
How it works
blocks.note: Up to 69, French works like English: tens + units. From 70, French counts on from 60, then in twenties.

blocks.title: Three spelling rules
blocks.body:
**1. Et un.** For 21, 31, 41, 51 and 61, French says **et un** (and one), without hyphens: [[vingt et un]], [[trente et un]], [[soixante et un]]. 71 is [[soixante et onze]] (60 and 11). But 81 and 91 have **no** et: [[quatre-vingt-un]], [[quatre-vingt-onze]].

**2. Hyphens.** All other numbers under 100 are joined with hyphens: [[vingt-deux]], [[quarante-huit]], [[soixante-quinze]], [[quatre-vingt-dix-neuf]].

**3. The s of quatre-vingts.** [[Quatre-vingts]] (80) has an **s**, but only when nothing follows: [[quatre-vingt-trois]] (83) has no s.

Since a 1990 spelling reform, you may also see hyphens everywhere: [[vingt-et-un]], [[soixante-et-onze]]. That is accepted too, but the traditional spelling above is still the most common.

blocks.title: Saying a price
blocks.note: French says the whole amount, then the cents as a plain number, without “and” or “cents”. Ask the price with [[C'est combien ?]] or [[Ça coûte combien ?]].

blocks.title: Phone numbers: France vs Canada
blocks.body:
**In France**, phone numbers have ten digits written in **pairs**: **06 71 84 92 37**. People read them in pairs too: [[zéro six, soixante et onze, quatre-vingt-quatre, quatre-vingt-douze, trente-sept]]. So you need all the numbers up to 99 to understand a French phone number!

**In Canada**, numbers are written **3-3-4**: **613-555-4798** or **(613) 555-4798**. The area code and the next three digits are usually said **digit by digit**: [[six, un, trois, cinq, cinq, cinq]]. For the last four digits, you will hear both: digit by digit ([[quatre, sept, neuf, huit]]) or two pairs ([[quarante-sept, quatre-vingt-dix-huit]]).

If you are not sure, ask: [[Vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ?]] or repeat the number back and ask [[C'est bien ça ?]]

blocks.title: Prices in Canada
blocks.body:
In French, the **decimal point is a comma**, and the currency symbol goes **after** the number, with a space: **31,50 $** (English Canada writes $31.50). You read both the same way: [[trente et un dollars cinquante]].

In everyday Québec French you may also hear [[une piasse]] for a dollar and [[une cenne]] for a cent ([[des cennes]]). These are informal words: recognize them, but say [[dollar]] and [[cent]] yourself.

blocks.title: Septante and nonante
blocks.body:
In **Belgium** and **Switzerland**, French speakers use simpler words for 70 and 90:

- [[septante]] = 70 (instead of [[soixante-dix]])
- [[nonante]] = 90 (instead of [[quatre-vingt-dix]])
- In parts of Switzerland, [[huitante]] = 80. Belgium keeps [[quatre-vingts]].

So a Belgian says [[septante-cinq]] for 75 and [[nonante-neuf]] for 99. **Learn to recognize these words, but don't use them in Canada or France**: there, people say [[soixante-dix]], [[quatre-vingts]] and [[quatre-vingt-dix]].

- **Vingt**: alone it sounds like “van”. In [[vingt et un]] and from [[vingt-deux]] to [[vingt-neuf]], you hear the *t*: “vant-duh”. But in [[quatre-vingt-un]], [[quatre-vingt-deux]]… the *t* stays silent.
- **Soixante**: the *x* sounds like *s*: “swa-sant”.
- **Cent**: silent *t*, “san”, except before a vowel: [[cent euros]] “san-t-euros”.
- **Quatre-vingts ans**: the s links with a *z*: “katr-van-z-an”.

blocks.title: Listen and repeat
blocks.note: Repeat each number out loud. Say 70–99 slowly at first: they are long!

summary:
- Count from [[vingt et un]] to [[cent]], with [[et un]], hyphens and [[quatre-vingts]] spelled correctly
- Understand 70–99: [[soixante-dix]], [[quatre-vingts]], [[quatre-vingt-dix]] (and recognize Belgian/Swiss [[septante]], [[nonante]])
- Say and understand prices: [[trente et un dollars cinquante]], [[C'est combien ?]]
- Give and check a phone number the French way (pairs) and the Canadian way (digits)
